# The Brake Pedal Goes to the Floor: Diagnosing a Hydraulic Leak vs. Master Cylinder Failure

When you swap out brake lines and bleed a system on a 1992 Cadillac DeVille, only to find the pedal drops instantly upon starting the engine, the problem isn't in the plumbing anymore. You have successfully eliminated external leaks at the wheel cylinders and likely cleared trapped air from static reservoirs. The fact that the pedal feels hard when the car is off confirms the master cylinder check valve is holding pressure initially. However, the moment the engine starts and you apply pressure, the system depressurizes immediately. This behavior points to two distinct failure modes: a catastrophic internal leak in the master cylinder or a collapsed ABS modulator (if equipped).

The most probable culprit is the hydraulic section of the master cylinder itself. In many vehicles from this era, the check valve that prevents fluid from draining back into the reservoir fails internally once the engine creates vacuum assist or when the pump cycles. When you pump the pedal with the car off, you are building pressure against a closed system. Once the engine starts, the brake booster engages, creating a significant vacuum behind the master cylinder pushrod. If the internal seals within the master cylinder cannot hold this differential pressure, fluid is drawn back from the wheel cylinders into the reservoir through the primary seal or via the check valve seat.

To diagnose this without immediate replacement, you can perform a "hold test" that isolates the components. With the car on level ground and the parking brake engaged, pump the pedal until it bottoms out firmly. Hold your foot there. Wait exactly 30 seconds. Release the pedal and observe if it returns to its resting position or if it sinks slightly. If it holds firm, the issue might be related to the power booster vacuum leak rather than hydraulic failure. However, if you start the engine while maintaining that pressure on the pedal, or if the pedal sinks rapidly after releasing, you have confirmed an internal bypass.

Some owners attempt to cross-bleed the system, as suggested in your case history. While cross-bleeding is a valid technique for removing air trapped in hard-to-reach corners of long lines, it cannot fix a master cylinder that is actively pumping fluid back into its own reservoir. The "fluid" you are bleeding out might be fresh brake fluid that has just been sucked from the wheel cylinders due to internal leakage.

If your DeVille does not have an Anti-lock Braking System (ABS), and the master cylinder fails this internal leak test, the solution is straightforward but costly: replace the entire unit. On a 1992 model, you will likely need a combination unit that integrates both front and rear hydraulic circuits, or two separate units depending on the specific trim level. Ensure you match the bore size and mounting bracket to your existing setup. Using a single-circuit master cylinder for a four-wheel drive vehicle without verifying the proportioning valve integration is a common mistake that leads to lock-up issues.

If your vehicle is ABS-equipped, the diagnosis becomes more complex. The modulator assembly contains the wheel cylinders and the hydraulic control unit. A failure here could manifest similarly to a standard brake system leak. You must inspect the ABS pump/motor for signs of overheating or electrical faults that might cause the solenoid valves to stick open. In some cases, the internal seals within the ABS modulator fail, allowing fluid to bypass the wheel cylinders and return to the reservoir when the pump is active.

Before concluding it is purely hydraulic failure, verify the brake booster vacuum hose. A cracked diaphragm in the booster can allow engine vacuum to bleed off into the atmosphere, reducing assist but not necessarily causing a total loss of pressure unless there is also an internal master cylinder leak. Disconnect the pushrod from the master cylinder and see if the pedal still sinks when you apply foot pressure. If it holds without the pushrod connected, the issue is strictly in the booster or the hydraulic section of the master cylinder.

Replacing the master cylinder on a 1992 Cadillac is a labor-intensive task involving the removal of the brake lines from the frame rails. Always use new copper crush washers and ensure the banjo bolts are torqued to manufacturer specifications to prevent future leaks at the firewall or chassis mount points.
